cues.text: In 1597, a man involved in a series of sacrilegious thefts from churches around Alcala de Henares, Spain, went to confess at the Jesuit church there, overcome with remorse for what he and his companions had done.
Among the stolen goods he brought forward were consecrated Hosts, taken from more than one church during their raids.
Rather than have the returned Hosts consumed immediately, the confessor grew cautious.
Priests in nearby Murcia and Segovia had recently been poisoned through contaminated Hosts.
He wanted to rule out any similar danger before allowing them near the altar again.
He had the Hosts sealed instead in a silver box, intending to observe over time whether they would decompose as ordinary bread naturally would.
Father Luis de la Palma, then rector of the Jesuit college, later had the sealed Hosts moved to a damp low chapel behind the sacristy and placed unconsecrated hosts alongside them for comparison.
Within months the unconsecrated hosts had visibly decomposed in the damp conditions, while the consecrated Hosts beside them showed no sign of deterioration at all.
The consecrated Hosts remained under observation for roughly a decade.
Sources differ on the precise number recovered and the exact span of years involved, but agree they were still perfectly intact well after ordinary bread would have decayed.
In 1615, by then serving as Jesuit provincial, Palma returned to Alcala and had formal testimony taken of the phenomenon.

The Hosts were preserved and venerated at Alcala for centuries afterward, but were hidden for safekeeping during the anticlerical violence of the Spanish Civil War in 1936, and their present whereabouts remain unknown.
What survives is the documented method behind the finding: a deliberate, controlled comparison against ordinary bread.
It was undertaken specifically to rule out a natural explanation before anyone called it miraculous, showing investigative caution unusual among Eucharistic accounts of this era.
